newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Billionaire Bronfman takes on the Swiss.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Billionaire Bronfman takes on the Swiss.

text.p: If only the Swiss bankers had offered him a chair, and if only they had not offered him $30 million to shut up and go away.

So muses billionaire Edgar Bronfman, who as president of the World Jewish Congress has spearheaded a campaign to force Swiss banks to make amends for refusing to turn over accounts opened by Holocaust victims in the 1930s and '40s. Faced with complaints from hundreds of heirs that the Swiss were making it impossible to retrieve the accounts, Bronfman launched a compensation campaign that in less than two years has turned into a public relations nightmare for once-proud Swiss banks.

As recounted in a recent interview and in his new book, "The Making of a Jew," Bronfman flew to meet the Swiss Bankers Association in September 1995 and was taken to an empty room. "I was stunned, we were all standing there in a room with no furniture -- it was rather rude behavior on their part," he said, recalling that when he asked the bankers for an accounting they read him a statement that Swiss bankers were ready to hand over about $30 million to settle the matter.
"I said, 'I didn't come here to discuss money. I want to discuss process.' And that stunned (them)," Bronfman said.

Battling the Swiss was not Bronfman's first international fight on behalf of Holocaust victims or world Jewry. Shortly after taking over the World Jewish Congress in 1981, he led an international campaign against former U.N. Secretary General Kurt Waldheim for covering up his past activities as "part and parcel of the Nazi killing machine." He also successfully negotiated with Soviet leaders to ease their severe restrictions on Jewish emigration.
AVOIDED RELIGION FOR YEARS

But he said being in the forefront of Jewish issues was something that came late to him because for many years he tried to deny his Jewish identity. The Canadian-born Bronfman, whose father founded the Seagram liquor empire, said he did his best as a young man to blend in with gentiles, from attending Protestant private schools to playing at a Quebec golf course that would not let Jews in the clubhouse.

Seeking to distance himself from his father, Samuel, whom he feared, Bronfman raised his first five children while shunning the most important traditions and tenets of Judaism. In defiance of his father, he contravened the Jewish prohibition against eating pork, compounding the transgression by doing so on a Jewish High Holiday.
"I was simply in rebellion against my father and I actually went so far as to eat ham at our house on Yom Kippur," Bronfman said.

After his father died in 1971, Bronfman, then 42, found himself chief executive of Seagram, one of North America's wealthiest men and about to embark on a journey of discovery about Judaism. Although he had been involved in charities and fund-raising for Israel since the early 1950s, he was not motivated then by a personal affinity for the Jewish religion.

That changed when Nahum Goldmann, founder of the World Jewish Congress (WJC), recruited Bronfman as chairman of the lobby group's North American branch. By 1981, Bronfman had been elected president of the WJC, a post he retains, and was building a reputation as a man who could open doors to some of the world's top decision makers, including Margaret Thatcher, George Bush, Golda Meir and Bill Clinton.
CALLED RABIN A FRIEND
Bronfman has fond memories of many of them, especially slain Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, whose murder in 1995 left him despairing for Middle East peace.

Bronfman's globetrotting diplomacy found him embracing his Jewish heritage, but his interest in Judaism came much later. The pivotal moment was in the late 1980s during a Moscow-bound flight with Israel Singer, an Orthodox rabbi and professor who is WJC secretary general.

Bronfman's curiosity about Singer's reading of the daily portion of Talmud -- writings on Jewish civil and religious law -- grew into a commitment to read the Torah. For Bronfman, it was the beginning of a learning process about Judaism that continues through e-mail correspondence with Singer.
Although still the nominal head of Seagram, Bronfman appears more willing to do what his father could not bring himself to do, pass the corporate reins to a new generation.

His son, Edgar Jr., 41, has been president and chief executive of Seagram since June 1994 and is credited with spearheading the company's push into entertainment. Bronfman said he had no regrets about his son's decision in mid-1995 to sell Seagram's 25 percent stake in DuPont to acquire 80 percent of MCA, now known as Universal Studios.
"I think he's doing a brilliant job," Bronfman said.

Meanwhile, the senior Bronfman, a U.S. citizen, plans to press on with efforts to establish compensation funds for Holocaust victims whose assets were confiscated. It is a mission made all the more pressing by the passage of time.
"What we have to do is write the last chapter," he said. "We will get the story, there is no question of that. But in the meantime, Holocaust survivors are dying every day."
